newsitem.title: UK: Full text of Nov UK purchasing managers survey.
newsitem.headline: Full text of Nov UK purchasing managers survey.

text.p: Following is the full text of the November Report on Business (Purchasing Managers' Survey) of the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS).
PMI REFLECTS FURTHER EXPANSION OF MANUFACTURING SECTOR. NEW ORDERS AND OUTPUT RISE SHARPLY. STRONGER POUND LEADS TO LOWER INPUT COSTS.
The Purchasing Managers' Index reflected expansion in the manufacturing sector for the sixth consecutive month in November.
The main driving forces behind the latest expansion were the continued strong growth in output and a further acceleration in the rate of growth of new orders.

The improvement in order books occurred in spite of the recent rise in the sterling exchange rate. The stronger pound was reported to have dampened overseas demand for certain goods somewhat by making UK products more expensive in overseas markets. (Against a trade weighted basket of currencies, sterling rose by around 10% between August and November). However, greater demand for goods in the domestic market more than made up for any export losses.

Order levels for consumer goods again showed the sharpest rise (as they have done throughout the recent growth revival), prompting producers of these goods to further boost output and employment levels. The increase in the rate of production of consumer goods was offset, however, by slightly slower growth in the production of non-consumer goods (investment goods and components) -- in part a reflection of uncertainty about future business conditions. This uncertainty was also reflected in employment, which rose only modestly in November.

The exchange rate also affected prices paid for inputs. Prices fell for the thirteenth month in a row in November, with purchasing managers seeing their average input prices fall to a greater extent than in the previous month. This represents a turnaround from the findings between August and October, when the rate at which prices were falling was found to have steadily eased. The recent increase in deflationary pressures was almost entirely a result of the stronger pound making imported inputs cheaper in sterling terms.

The availability of inputs generally remained good, although just under 10% of firms saw delivery times lengthen as suppliers incurred delays in meeting order levels. These generally good supply conditions allowed purchasing managers to hold lower stocks of inputs in order to cut costs.

* The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing economy and acts as a leading indicator for the whole economy. The indicator is derived from individual diffusion indices which measure changes in output, new orders, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of goods purchased. A reading of the PMI below 50% indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining; above 50%, that it is generally expanding. The seasonally adjusted index may be subject to revision as improved estimation of seasonal adjustments occur with each month's new data.
OUTPUT

The Output Index recorded a strong increase again in November, although the rate of growth dipped slightly for the second month running. Growth in output of consumer goods (which has led the recovery over the past six months from the mid-1994 to early-1996 slowdown) continued to accelerate. Growth in output of investment goods and components, although still strong, was slightly weaker than in October.
NEW ORDERS

The seasonally adjusted rate of growth of new orders accelerated for the sixth successive month (although the New Orders Index has yet to reach levels seen in 1994). The increase in November was driven by stronger demand for consumer goods and components. Export orders continued to grow, but the recent strengthening of sterling was reported to have reduced some sales, especially for components.
QUANTITY OF PURCHASES

The Quantity of Purchases Index registered a substantial increase in the amount of goods bought by companies in November. Producers of consumer goods showed the largest rise, as faster production rates depleted existing stocks of materials. Producers of investment goods, on the contrary, continued to deliberately run down stock levels by restricting growth in purchasing activity below the rate of growth of output.
PRICES

The Prices Index, which had shown some signs of picking up between August and October, dropped again in November, as over a fifth of all companies saw prices fall. Although the prices of some goods bought in the UK continued to harden as demand picked up, the recent strengthening of sterling was reported to have reduced the prices paid for many imported materials.
SUPPLIERS' DELIVERY TIMES

The seasonally adjusted Delivery Times Index fell for the sixth consecutive month in November, dropping to its lowest level for sixteen months. The index has been below 50.0 in each of the past three months, signalling a lengthening of suppliers' delivery times. This lengthening was due to the fact that suppliers have become busier meeting manufacturers' increased input requirements.
STOCKS OF PURCHASES

The seasonally adjusted Stocks of Purchases Index rose very slightly but continued to signal one of the sharpest declines in stock levels yet recorded by this survey. With the availability of most inputs generally remaining good and prices (especially for imported inputs) continuing to fall, companies have been able to save costs by further running down stock levels to more efficient levels.
STOCKS OF FINISHED GOODS

Manufacturers continued to focus upon holding levels of finished goods stock as low as possible in November for cost considerations. Inventories of consumer, investment and intermediary goods all fell again as deliberate policies to run stocks more efficiently were often exaggerated by depletion through higher than expected sales.
EMPLOYMENT

The seasonally adjusted Employment Index recorded further modest growth in November. Although firms across all Report on Business sectors have been raising output to meet demand, many firms remained uncertain about future business conditions and chose to continue trimming workforces (especially intermediate goods producers).
INDICES BY MARKET SECTOR
CONSUMER GOODS

The rate of growth of new orders, output and employment accelerated in the consumer goods sector. This sector has recorded the fastest growth in order levels throughout the whole of this year, with companies increasingly benefiting from improved export demand during recent months in spite of the strengthened pound. The increased rate of production depleted stocks of purchases, prompting a further significant increase in the quantity of goods purchased during the month. Suppliers to these producers were, in some instances, slow to meet the increased requirements, leading to a further lengthening of delivery times. Although the stronger pound had little adverse effect on export demand, firms benefited from lower prices of imported goods.
INVESTMENT/CAPITAL GOODS

The investment goods sector continued to expand in November. Output of investment goods rose sharply -- the third significant consecutive monthly rise (albeit at a more modest rate of growth compared with October). Both purchasing activity and employment rose to support the increased output and meet further growth in demand. Order levels rose for the fifth month in a row in November, but weakness in export markets was found to have led to a decline in the rate of growth of new orders. Supply of goods remained generally good while prices fell again. With few fears of shortages and a favourable outlook on input prices, purchasing managers generally chose to deplete current stocks of purchases for cost saving purposes.
INTERMEDIATE GOODS

New orders for intermediate goods (components) rose for the sixth month running in November, recording the largest monthly increase since October 1994. The improvement in demand came largely from the domestic market, especially from producers of consumer goods rebuilding their stocks of components. Export demand rose but only very slightly. This Report on Business sector found the stronger pound to have had the most significant adverse effect on overseas orders. On the plus side, prices fell sharply again as imported inputs became cheaper in sterling terms.
This was, however, the only sector to reduce employment levels, largely reflecting uncertainty about future business conditions.
